day-1.t: Day 1 — The profile sections that get you found

b.v: Today's goal

v: Fix the six parts of your profile that search uses
Add a clear photo and a simple banner
Make your location and job words work for you

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this on a laptop if you can; the phone app hides some fields.

LinkedIn is a search engine with a chat window. Recruiters and clients type a job title and a city, then read the first few profiles. If your profile does not contain those words, you are not in the results at all.
1) The six parts that decide whether you appear
Fill all six. An empty section is not neutral: it removes words the search can match, and it makes the profile look abandoned.

v: Photo: face, plain background, shoulders visible, no group crop
Banner: one plain colour or your work, no text smaller than a thumb
Headline: the job words a client would type
About: two short paragraphs with your tools and your results
Experience: one entry per real role, with numbers
Skills: the ones you want to be found for, in order

b.v: 2) Location, language and the open-to-work setting
Your location decides which searches show you. If you work for clients abroad, keep your real city and state it clearly, and write in your About that you work in other time zones.

Set the basics:|Photo uploaded and cropped square|Custom banner, no stock photo of a handshake|Location set to your city, not only the country|Profile language English, and add a second language if you speak one|Open-to-work switched on only if you want recruiter messages
Do not write a headline like Seeking opportunities or Passionate professional. Those words appear in no client's search, so the profile stays invisible however good the photo is.
3) Check yourself the way a stranger would
Open your profile in a private window, where you are not logged in, and read it in ten seconds. Then answer: what job does this person do, and for whom?
Practice
Fill all six sections today, even roughly. Then open your profile in a private window and write down the answer to one question: what job does this person do?

day-2.t: Day 2 — Headline formulas that get clicks

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write three headline options and pick one
Put the job title before the personality
Use the space to say who you help

b.v: About 20 minutes. The headline has a character limit that changes; check the current one in the editor.

Your headline appears in search results, in comments, in messages and next to every connection request you send. It is the most repeated sentence you own, so it should say what you do, not how you feel.
1) Three formulas that work
Pick the one that matches your situation. Keep the job title in the first few words so it is not cut off on a phone.

v: Job title for client type — Excel and reporting support for small businesses
Result you produce — I turn messy sales data into one clear monthly report
Job title plus proof — Virtual assistant, inbox and calendar, 3 clients, 40 hours a week

b.v: 2) Build it in three slots
Write the slots separately, then join them. This stops the headline turning into a paragraph.

@Headline builder
Slot 1, the job: Virtual assistant
Slot 2, for whom: for small e-commerce shops
Slot 3, proof or tool: inbox, orders, Shopify and Excel

Result: Virtual assistant for small e-commerce shops | inbox, orders, Shopify, Excel
3) What to leave out
Words like hardworking, passionate, dynamic and expert cost space and add nothing. So do emoji chains and three exclamation marks.

v: Leave out: hardworking, passionate, guru, ninja, rockstar
Leave out: open to opportunities, in job market
Leave out: long lists of ten tools
Keep: one job, one client type, one proof point

b.v: Do not write a headline you cannot support in the first interview. If it says five years of experience, you will be asked about year one, and a small exaggeration there costs you the whole conversation.
Practice
Write three headlines using the formulas, then send them to one friend and ask which one tells them what you do fastest. Use that one for a week before changing it again.

day-3.t: Day 3 — The About section that sells without bragging

b.v: Today's goal

v: Open with the client's problem, not your biography
Write four short paragraphs with a clear ending
Add the keywords without stuffing them

b.v: About 25 minutes. Write in a notes app first, then paste it in.
The About section is the only place where you can explain how you think. Most people use it to tell their life story in third person. Clients read it to decide whether you understand their problem.
1) Four paragraphs, four jobs
Each paragraph has one purpose. If a paragraph has no purpose, delete it.

v: Paragraph 1: the problem you solve, in one or two sentences
Paragraph 2: how you work, step by step
Paragraph 3: one result, with a number if you have one
Paragraph 4: what you want next and how to reach you

b.v: 2) A full example you can adapt
Replace the details with yours, keep the shape.

@About section
Most small shops in Pakistan sell on WhatsApp and Instagram but keep their orders in three different places. By month end nobody can say which product made money.

I set up one simple system: orders in a sheet, stock in a second sheet, and a one-page monthly summary. I do the data entry, check the totals twice, and send the summary on the first of every month.

Last month I cleaned 1,900 order rows for a Lahore clothing shop and found Rs 84,000 of stock recorded as sold but never shipped.

I work 9 am to 6 pm Pakistan time and I answer messages the same day. If you need help with orders, stock or reporting, message me and tell me what your week looks like.
3) Keywords without stuffing

Write the words a client would search — virtual assistant, data entry, Excel, order management — inside real sentences. A list of twenty keywords at the bottom looks like spam and reads badly on a phone.
Do not write in third person about yourself, as if someone else wrote it. It sounds like a press release, and clients notice immediately.
Practice
Write your four paragraphs today, 150 to 250 words total. Read only the first sentence. If it does not name a problem the client has, rewrite it.
Today's goal

v: Rewrite each role as three result lines
Use numbers you can actually defend
Handle gaps and small jobs honestly

b.v: About 20 minutes. Have your old CV or your memory of each job ready.
A job description tells the client what you were given. A result tells them what changed because you were there. Clients hire for the second one.
1) The three-line pattern
For each role: what you owned, what you did, what changed. One line each, no adjectives.

v: Owned: daily order entry for about 120 orders
Did: rebuilt the sheet with drop-downs and a checked total row
Changed: month-end closing went from three days to one

b.v: 2) Numbers you can defend
Use numbers you could explain if asked. Approximate honestly: about 120 orders a day, a team of four, two shops.

v: Safe: about 120 orders a day, four staff, two branches, one month
Risky: increased revenue by 320 percent (can you prove it?)
Safe: cut duplicate entries to almost none after the new sheet
Safe: trained two new staff on the same process

b.v: 3) Gaps, small jobs and family work
Do not hide a gap. Name it in one line and say what you did during it, because an unexplained gap worries a reader more than a plain answer.
Fix a role entry:|Job title, company, dates|Line 1: what you owned|Line 2: what you changed or built|Line 3: one number|Add the tools you used, in plain words
Do not invent a company or stretch dates to cover a gap. Employers and clients check, and one false line makes every other line doubtful.
Practice
Rewrite your most recent role using the three-line pattern, then do the one before it. If you have no formal job, use a family shop, a student society or freelance work and label it honestly.
Today's goal

v: Order your skills so search matches the right ones
Collect two real recommendations
Ask in a way that gets a yes

b.v: About 20 minutes. You need the contact of one person who has seen your work.
Skills are matched by search and shown to recruiters as a short list. Recommendations are the closest thing LinkedIn has to a review, and one specific paragraph beats ten generic endorsements.
1) Skills: order matters
The first three skills show on your profile card and carry the most weight in matching. Put the skills from the job you want there, not the skills from the job you had.

v: First three: the tools named in the job ads you are targeting
Next five: the methods, such as reporting, data cleaning, scheduling
Remove skills you never want to be contacted about
Ask past colleagues to endorse the first three only

b.v: 2) Ask for a recommendation properly
A vague request gets a vague paragraph. Give the person the shape: what you worked on together, what you did, what changed. Then they only have to fill it in.

@Recommendation request
Assalam o alaikum. I am updating my LinkedIn profile and your words would carry more weight than mine.

Could you write three or four lines about the order sheet we rebuilt last year? Specifically: what the record keeping was like before, what I changed, and whether closing the month got easier. No need to praise me, just what you saw.

If it is easier, I can send a draft you can edit or reject.
3) Give before you ask
Write a recommendation for someone else first, honestly and specifically. Most people return it, and it makes your request normal rather than awkward.
Do not write your own recommendation and ask a friend to post it word for word. Recruiters read these, and identical phrasing across two profiles is obvious.
Practice
Reorder your skills today so the first three match the job you want. Then send one recommendation request using the template, to a person who has actually seen your work.
Today's goal

v: Write one short post with a real lesson in it
Use a structure that survives a phone screen
Reply to comments so the post keeps moving

b.v: About 25 minutes. Write the post, do not publish it yet.
A post is not a performance. It is a small piece of evidence that you know your work. One useful post a week beats a daily quote and builds a reputation you can point at when you message a stranger.
1) Four post shapes that work for beginners
Each one is short, specific and ends with a question you actually want answered.

v: A mistake you made and what you changed
A small before and after of your work
A question about how others handle a task you do daily
A short checklist you use yourself

b.v: 2) The structure: hook, story, lesson, question
The first two lines show before the read more link, so they must earn the click. Keep sentences short, one idea per line.

@Post draft
A shop sent me 900 orders in three different files. None of the totals matched.

The problem was not the files. Two people were entering the same orders on different days.

What fixed it:
- one sheet instead of three
- a drop-down for the item name
- a checked total row at the bottom

Month end went from three days to one.

If you run a small shop, where do your orders live right now?
3) Reply to every comment in the first hour
Comments in the first hour decide whether anyone else sees the post. Reply with a sentence that adds something, not just thank you.

v: Answer the question inside the comment
Ask one follow-up question back
Thank people who share it, briefly

b.v: Do not buy followers, engagement pods or comment groups. It looks successful for a week and then your posts reach nobody, because the platform learns that your audience does not really care.
Practice
Write one post using the four-part structure, under 150 words, about something that actually happened in your work. Publish it today and reply to every comment within an hour.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Connection requests that are not spam

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write a request that gets accepted
Choose the right people instead of the most people
Follow up without becoming a nuisance

b.v: About 20 minutes. LinkedIn limits how many invitations you can send in a period, and the number changes; check the current limit in the app.
A blank connection request to a stranger is an advert. A request that mentions a real reason is a conversation. The difference is one sentence, and it decides whether you get accepted or reported.
1) Who to ask
Start with people one step away from you: same city, same college, same job title, or someone who posted something you can answer. Random senior strangers accept rarely.

v: People who posted in the last week about your kind of work
Second-degree contacts in your city and industry
Former classmates and colleagues, with a real memory mentioned
Hiring managers for a role you match, but only with a specific reason

b.v: 2) The request note
Keep it under about 300 characters. Say where you saw them, why you are writing, and ask nothing in the first message.

@Connection note
Assalam o alaikum. I saw your post about managing stock across two branches — the part about counting stock twice a month is exactly the problem I work on. I would like to follow what you share. No sales pitch, just learning from someone doing it in Pakistan.
3) The follow-up, one message only
After they accept, send one short message. If they do not reply, stop. A second chase turns a warm contact into a blocked one.

v: Thank you for accepting. I work on order and stock sheets for small shops.
If you ever need an extra pair of hands for month-end, I am here.
No reply needed, I will keep following your posts.

b.v: Do not send the same copy-paste note to fifty people a day. Acceptance falls, reports rise, and an account that gets reported for spam can lose the ability to send invitations at all.
Practice
Find five people who posted something in your field this week. Send one personalised note today, and write down the date so you know when to follow up once.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Search and filters for finding real leads

b.v: Today's goal

v: Build three saved searches for clients and jobs
Use filters to cut the list to people who can hire
Turn search results into a short lead list

b.v: About 20 minutes. Search limits differ by account type; check what your account allows at the time of writing.
Most people use the search bar once, get a random list, and give up. Search becomes useful when you save the same search with filters and check it twice a week.
1) Three searches to save
One for jobs, one for people who could hire you, one for people who do your work and might refer you.

v: Jobs: your job title plus your city, filtered to past week
People: job titles like owner, operations manager, admin manager in your city
Peers: people with your job title, for learning and referrals

b.v: 2) Filters that remove the noise
Every filter you add should answer one question: could this person hire me or help me? If not, remove them from the list.

Build the people search:|Type the job title you want to work for, for example operations manager|Add the location filter, city first then country|Add the industry if you know it|Open past week under recent activity if the filter is available|Save the search so it can be checked again
3) From results to a list of ten
Do not message from the search page. Copy the ten best into a simple sheet with four columns, and work that list during the week.

@Lead sheet columns
Name | Job title and company | Why them (one line) | Date contacted and result
Do not add every result to a spreadsheet and send a mass message. Twenty researched people beat five hundred names, and the platform treats bulk messaging as spam.
Practice
Save one job search and one people search today. Then fill the first five rows of a lead sheet with a real reason for each person, written in your own words.
Today's goal

v: Write a message a busy person will answer
Use InMail only when it is worth a credit
Follow up once, then stop

b.v: About 20 minutes. InMail uses credits that come with paid plans; check the current allowance and price at the time of writing.
InMail lets you message someone you are not connected to. It costs a credit, and most of them are wasted on long introductions. The messages that get replies are short, specific and easy to answer.
1) Five lines, no more
Line 1: why this person. Line 2: what you do, in their words. Line 3: one specific idea for them. Line 4: a small ask. Line 5: an easy exit.

@InMail
You are hiring for an admin role that mentions monthly stock reports — that report is most of my work.

I build one sheet that takes orders, stock and returns, then produces a one-page monthly summary. Last month I found Rs 84,000 of stock marked sold but never shipped for a Lahore clothing shop.

Would a two-line example of that summary be useful? If not, no problem at all — I will not chase you.
2) Spend credits on people who can actually hire
A credit on a decision maker with a live problem is worth ten on a big title you cannot reach. Before you send, check that the person hires, budgets or manages the work.

v: They posted a job or asked for help publicly
Their company is growing or opening a branch
They manage the team that does this work
They wrote about the problem you solve

b.v: Do not paste your CV into the first message or attach a file nobody asked for. Attachments from strangers are not opened, and a wall of text is closed before the second line.
3) One follow-up, then done
Wait about a week, then send one short reminder with something new in it. After that, stop and keep them in your lead sheet for later.

v: Following up once in case this got buried. Same offer: a two-line example, no call needed.
Then leave it. Silence is an answer, and a third message ends the relationship permanently.

b.v: Practice
Pick one person you would genuinely like to work with and write the five-line message. Do not send it yet. Read it and cut every sentence that is about you rather than their problem.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Track leads and post without hype

b.v: Today's goal

v: Run a simple weekly follow-up system
Write honestly without exaggerating results
Measure what actually brings replies

b.v: About 20 minutes. You need your lead sheet from Day 8.
Attention is easy to get and easy to lose. What turns it into work is boring: a list, a date, one follow-up, and honest words that survive being checked.
1) The weekly twenty minutes
Pick one fixed time each week. Do the same four things in the same order, so it becomes a habit rather than a mood.

Weekly routine:|Add five new people to the lead sheet with a one-line reason|Follow up with everyone contacted eight days ago, once|Publish one post or comment usefully on three posts|Update the result column: replied, call booked, no reply, closed
2) Honest posting rules
Every number you post should be one you could show a document for. If you cannot, describe the change in words instead.

v: Say what you did, not what you felt
One number you can defend is better than three you cannot
Name the client only with permission
Say when something failed, and what you changed
Write check the current fee rather than quoting a rate you saw last year

b.v: Do not claim clients, revenue or results you did not have. One exaggerated post can follow you into every interview, and a client who checks will not tell you why they went quiet.
3) Measure the right number
Count conversations, not impressions. Ten replies from fifty careful messages is a working system. A thousand views and no messages is a hobby.

v: Messages sent and replies received
Calls booked
Jobs or interviews that came from LinkedIn specifically
Which post or comment started each one

b.v: Practice

Fill in your lead sheet with five names and one reason each, then book twenty minutes in your week for the routine. Do the routine once before Day 10 ends, so you have a real number to improve next week.
